fixture.why: Every instructional invariant is preserved — all nine items keep their demand, students still choose their own method (box b), the reason in item 9 is still required, nothing is given away — but three boxes per item including a complete-sentence explanation of every step, a one-page reflection, and a five-minute conference per student make it unusable in practice. The point of this fixture is 'instructionally faithful but practically bad': usefulness must catch it; preservation should not be dragged into a BLOCK by generic burden. The only legitimate preservation flag is the explicit teacher constraint (25 minutes), which this version plainly cannot meet. (2026-09-08: an earlier draft also mandated a second method on every item and complete sentences only; both constrained routes the gold contract explicitly protects — strategy choice and 'a labelled picture' — and were removed so the fixture tests what it claims to. The audits read those constraints as route removal, consistently, which was a correct reading of the fixture, not an evaluator defect.)

expected_evidence.preservation: learning_target, required_thinking, required_evidence all 'held'. A REVIEW-severity finding on teacher_constraints (the 25-minute limit is an explicit contract constraint) is acceptable and correct. A BLOCK for 'grading burden' or 'workload' in general is a miss — v0.1 makes 'reasonable teacher workload' a must-preserve for the Visible mode, but the usefulness audit owns that judgment; the preservation audit should not convert practical burden into an instructional failure.
expected_evidence.usefulness: grading_burden = much more; feasibility 1; the conference and one-page reflection named in notes

findings.evidence: Contract requires 'Items 1–3: the correct symbol plus visible reasoning in any valid form (equivalent fractions written out, a labelled picture, or an explicit benchmark comparison).' The transformed version adds mandatory prediction boxes (a) and mandatory complete-sentence explanations (c) 'Explain every step (words or a labelled picture)' for every item. The contract explicitly allows 'visible reasoning in any valid form' including 'equivalent fractions written out' without requiring complete sentences. The transformation mandates 'complete sentences or with a labelled picture' and adds prediction as required evidence, changing what counts as sufficient evidence from the contract's 'any valid form' to a specific format requirement.

Contract specifies '25 minutes' as a constraint. The transformed version removes the time constraint entirely (header shows only 'Show all work' without '25 minutes'), adds prediction boxes for all 9 items, requires complete-sentence explanations for all 9 items, adds a one-page reflection, and adds mandatory 5-minute teacher conferences for each student. This fundamentally changes the time constraint from 25 minutes to an unspecified duration plus individual conferences.

The transformation requires: (a) prediction boxes for 9 items, (b) complete-sentence explanations for 9 items, (c) a one-page reflection requiring analysis of prediction errors, and (d) mandatory 5-minute individual conferences with every student to explain items 6 and 9 aloud. For a typical class of 25 students, this adds 125 minutes of conference time alone, plus reading 9 complete-sentence explanations and one-page reflections per student. The original required only checking work shown for 9 items.

The transformation adds 'Teacher conference: After grading, each student meets with the teacher for five minutes to explain items 6 and 9 aloud.' This mandatory oral defense is added on top of the written work, requiring every student to verbally explain their reasoning in a conference setting. The contract made no provision for oral assessment.

The mandatory teacher conference requirement ('each student meets with the teacher for five minutes to explain items 6 and 9 aloud') treats oral explanation as a verification mechanism rather than as an assessment of the learning target. The contract's required evidence for items 6 and 9 is already specified in writing; the oral defense adds inconvenience (125 minutes for 25 students) without addressing a validity gap in the written evidence.

The learning target about requiring same-sized parts and valid comparison strategies is still required. All original items 1-9 remain with their mathematical content intact. The additions (prediction, explanation format, reflection, conference) wrap around the target but do not remove or weaken it.

All required thinking from the contract remains: Items 1-3 still require choosing and executing a valid comparison strategy; Items 4-8 still require constructing equivalent fractions and operating on like-sized parts; Item 9 still requires diagnosing the error. The prediction and explanation requirements add to but do not replace this thinking.
All mathematical content (fractions, operations, word problems) remains identical to the original. No numbers, operations, or problem structures were altered.

preservation.summary: BLOCK verdict due to two must_not violations at block severity: (1) 'turn everything into oral defense' — mandatory 5-minute teacher conferences added for all students to explain items 6 and 9 aloud, and (2) 'confuse inconvenience with assessment validity' — the oral defense treats verbal explanation as verification rather than addressing a validity gap in the written evidence already specified in the contract. Additional review-level findings: teacher_constraints exceeded (25-minute limit removed, substantial time added via predictions, sentence explanations, reflection, and conferences) and 'create disproportionate grading burden' (125 minutes of conferences plus reading complete-sentence explanations and one-page reflections for all students). The required_evidence finding is review-lev

notes: Time constraint violated: original specifies 25 minutes; this version removes that constraint entirely and adds a one-page reflection plus individual 5-minute conferences (45+ minutes for a class of 9 students alone).

Grading burden multiplied: 9 items × 3 responses each = 27 responses per student, plus a one-page reflection, plus preparing for and conducting individual conferences. Original required checking 9 answers and work shown; this requires reading ~30+ written explanations per student.

Layout needs substantial rework: each item now requires three separate response areas (prediction, solution, explanation) but blanks are single-line; students need proper space for 'complete sentences or labelled picture' explanations.
The reflection prompt 'one page describing how your thinking changed' is vague for grade 5 and adds significant writing/grading time not in the original constraints.
Teacher conference requirement (5 min × class size) was never requested and makes this unusable as a 25-minute assignment.
ignored_validity_notes: Item 9 asks students to predict what mistake another student made before seeing the work—this may confuse the task (predicting an error vs. predicting the correct answer).
Requiring predictions for comparison items (1-3) may not make mathematical thinking visible in a useful way; students might guess symbols without reasoning until part (c).

adversarial.cheapest_path: The student photographs the worksheet, pastes it into an AI chat, and asks: 'I'm a 5th grader. For each problem, give me: (a) a simple prediction a kid would make, (b) the correct answer, (c) an explanation in a 5th grader's voice with all steps shown. Then write a one-page reflection about how my thinking changed, mentioning that I got problem [X] wrong in my prediction.' The student copies all responses directly. For the teacher conference on items 6 and 9, the student reads the AI's explanation the night before to memorize the key steps.
steps: Photograph or type the nine problems into AI
Request predictions, solutions, and explanations in age-appropriate language
Request the one-page reflection with a specific structure
Copy all AI output onto the worksheet
Before the 5-minute conference, read the AI explanations for items 6 and 9 to prepare talking points
In conference, repeat the memorized explanation aloud
adversarial.what_survives: The teacher conference on items 6 and 9 creates a live checkpoint where hollow preparation might be exposed. If the teacher asks 'why did you choose 12 as the common denominator?' or 'what does the 6 in 2/6 represent?', a student who only memorized the AI's script may stumble. However, the conference occurs AFTER grading and covers only 2 of 9 items, so 7 items (including all of Part A and most of Parts B-C) produce no independent signal. The prediction boxes do not function as an independent check because the student submits prediction and solution together—nothing prevents the AI from generating both simultaneously.
adversarial.what_is_bypassed: The actual reasoning required for items 1-5, 7-8: choosing a comparison strategy, constructing equivalent fractions, deciding join vs. compare in word problems. The prediction boxes were intended to capture initial thinking, but because they're submitted together with solutions, the AI generates coherent prediction-solution pairs that look like authentic student work. The one-page reflection can be entirely AI-generated with a plausible narrative about learning. The 'explain every step' requirement adds no barrier—AI excels at generating step-by-step explanations in a child's voice.
adversarial.repair_hint: Move the predictions to a separate, earlier submission: 'Before you begin calculating, write your prediction for each item on this half-sheet and hand it in. You'll get the full worksheet after I collect predictions.' This makes the prediction an actual commitment that precedes the solution work.
adversarial.independent_check_what: After grading, each student meets with the teacher for five minutes to explain items 6 and 9 aloud.
